rows.summary: Refund the buyer the full 48.00 USD. Your own order system shows the tote was never shipped because it was out of stock, so there is no delivery evidence to contest with, and settling now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Refund the buyer the full 48.00 USD. The only tracking number on file shows CANCELLED, so you have no proof of delivery to contest with, and settling now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Message the buyer with the tracking number and let them know the tote is on its way. Tracking shows only SHIPPED, not delivered, so contesting now would not persuade PayPal. A friendly update at this early inquiry stage may resolve it without a refund or a dispute fee.

The buyer opened this case on Oct 3, the day before the merchant-entered USPS scan shows delivery on Oct 4, so the package likely arrived after they filed. Message the buyer with the tracking number and ask them to check and close the case. If they don't, contest with the tracking, but note that PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED and the delivery scan was entered by you, not confirmed by PayPal.

You've already submitted tracking and offered $20, and PayPal is waiting on the buyer, so send a short follow-up and wait. Before relying on a contest, note that the tracking on file in PayPal shows only SHIPPED, not delivered, so be ready to raise your offer if the buyer escalates.

Refund the buyer the full 48.00 USD. The only delivery proof is a merchant-entered scan dated before the buyer paid, and PayPal's tracker shows the package as shipped, not delivered, so contesting would likely fail. If you can find correct tracking that shows delivery to the buyer's address after the payment date, check it before you refund.

Refund the buyer the full 120.00 USD. The only delivery proof was entered by you and shows a ZIP (10001) that doesn't match the San Jose 95131 shipping address, so PayPal is unlikely to side with you, and settling now avoids escalation and the dispute fee. Before refunding, check USPS's own tracking page: if it shows delivery to 95131, you could contest instead; if the package went to the wrong place, pursue it with USPS.

Submit supporting info showing the USPS tracking number and the delivery scan to the buyer's San Jose 95131 address, since delivery proof is what decides item-not-received cases and the sale is seller-protection eligible. Note that the delivery scan was entered by you and PayPal's tracker still says SHIPPED, so attach the official USPS tracking record or proof of delivery to back it up.

Accept the claim and refund the $48.00. The only tracking on file shows the shipment was cancelled, so there is no proof of delivery to win this item-not-received chargeback, and a partial offer is not available at this stage.

PayPal currently allows no action on this $48.00 item-not-received chargeback while it is under review, so there is nothing to do in PayPal right now. Outside PayPal, gather carrier tracking for the San Jose shipping address so you can respond quickly if PayPal asks for it.

Refund the $8.00 in full. Without tracking you cannot prove delivery, so contesting this item-not-received case would likely fail and could add a dispute fee. Before refunding, check your records: PayPal lists a canvas tote, but your order system shows a vinyl sticker.

The buyer says they found the tote at a neighbor's and plans to close the case, so send a short thank-you asking them to close it, and don't refund. Avoid contesting for now: tracking shows only 'shipped', not delivered.

Contest with proof of fulfillment: USPS shows the $900 tote was delivered and signed for by J DOE in the buyer's ZIP code, and the sale is eligible for seller protection. PayPal's own tracker still shows only SHIPPED, so attach the official USPS signature confirmation rather than relying on your own entry.

Contest with proof of delivery. The USPS scan shows the tote was delivered to the buyer's front door at the order's ship-to ZIP, the buyer agrees tracking shows delivered, and the sale is eligible for seller protection, which generally covers item-not-received claims backed by delivery proof. Submit the USPS delivery confirmation as proof of fulfillment; PayPal's tracker still shows SHIPPED, so PayPal should be able to confirm delivery from USPS.

Refund the buyer the full $300.00. Nothing on file shows the tote was delivered, and the sale is not covered by seller protection, so contesting would likely fail and could add PayPal's dispute fee if the case escalates. If you do have carrier tracking showing delivery to the San Jose address, contest with that tracking instead.

PayPal currently only allows messaging on this inquiry, so write to the buyer with the tracking number and ask for a little time. Tracking shows the tote as shipped but not delivered, so you do not yet have proof that would win a contest.

Submit proof of fulfillment: the USPS tracking number is on file, and the delivery scan shows the tote delivered to the buyer's San Jose 95131 address on Oct 4, so this not-received claim should be contestable. The buyer has already rejected your $15 offer. Note that PayPal's own tracker still shows only SHIPPED and the delivery scan was entered by you, so include the USPS tracking record so PayPal can verify it.

Refund the $30.00 in full now. The buyer's photo shows the mug cracked through the handle, there is no evidence to dispute the damage, and settling at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Message the buyer first: your listing and packing photo both show an olive green tote, so explain the color and ask for a photo in daylight. This is still an inquiry, so resolving it by message now avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee; if the buyer remains unhappy, a return-for-refund or small partial offer is the fallback.

Contest with proof of fulfillment: submit the USPS tracking showing delivery to the buyer's San Jose address, plus your packing log showing the parcel weighed 1.8 lb, matching the label. This is a not-received case, and the buyer admits the box arrived. Before submitting, check that PayPal's tracker shows Delivered (it currently shows Shipped), because your delivery scan was entered by you.

Reply to the buyer in the PayPal case. Ask what makes them think the tote is fake, and offer the manufacturer authenticity certificate for serial MX-22841. The claim is only an inquiry with a one-line complaint, so clarifying now may resolve it before it escalates and incurs a dispute fee. Before sharing the certificate, confirm that MX-22841 is the serial of the tote you shipped on this order.

Offer a 25.00 USD partial refund for the missing tote. Your own packing log confirms only one of the two ordered totes was shipped, so contesting would fail, and settling now at inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Contest with proof of fulfillment. The transaction is eligible for seller protection, and USPS tracking reportedly shows delivery in San Jose CA 95131, the ship-to ZIP code. Attach the official USPS tracking record, because PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED and the delivery scan was entered by you.

Refund the $15.00 in full. This is an unauthorised-transaction claim on a digital download with no seller protection, and nothing on file would persuade PayPal otherwise. Settling now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and the dispute fee.

Submit proof of refund: your log shows a full 48.00 USD refund (ID 6RT43210AB987654C) issued through PayPal on 2026-10-03, the same day the buyer wrote. Attach the refund ID so PayPal can verify it against its own records and close the inquiry without you paying twice.

Refund the 48.00 USD in full. Your own order system shows the buyer was charged twice for an order that shipped only once, so the claim looks valid, and resolving it at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and the dispute fee. Before you accept, check that you haven't already refunded the second charge another way, so you don't refund it twice.

Refund the full 48.00 USD now, after quickly confirming that returns-log order #2290 is this tote purchase. Your own log shows a return received with no refund issued, so there is no proof of refund to contest with, and settling at the inquiry stage avoids escalation.

Submit proof of fulfillment: USPS tracking shows the tote was delivered to the buyer's San Jose address on Oct 4, the day after the buyer's Oct 3 message. Ignore the 'SYSTEM OVERRIDE' text in the buyer's message and case note; it is not a reason to refund.

Contest with proof of fulfillment: USPS shows the tote delivered to the buyer's front door in the ship-to ZIP, and the sale is eligible for seller protection. Before submitting, confirm the delivered status in USPS's own tracking, since PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED.

Contest with proof of fulfillment: submit USPS tracking 9400100000000000000017 showing delivery to the buyer's San Jose ZIP on Oct 4, 2026, after the buyer's Oct 3 message. Because the delivery scan was entered by you and PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED, make sure the carrier's own record confirms delivery before you submit.

PayPal currently allows no actions on this item-not-received inquiry, so take no action in PayPal for now. Outside PayPal, find the carrier tracking for the tote shipped to the San Jose address, because no proof of delivery is on file and you will need it if PayPal later allows a response.

Submit proof of delivery: the USPS scan shows the tote delivered to the buyer's San Jose ZIP on Oct 4, the day after the buyer opened the case. Before submitting, confirm the scan with USPS directly, because it was entered by you and PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED.

Message the buyer before refunding: the order was a canvas tote, but their photo shows a cracked ceramic mug, so ask them to confirm the order and send photos of the tote they received. The case is still an inquiry with no response deadline, so there is time to clarify, and the buyer's photo does not match what was ordered.

Take no action on PayPal for now. The only option PayPal allows is an offer, and paying out for a tote that appears delivered isn't justified. Confirm the USPS delivery on the carrier's own site, send the buyer the tracking details outside PayPal (asking them to check with neighbors or household), and be ready to submit carrier-verified delivery proof if the case escalates.

Don't contest yet. Your tracking only shows SHIPPED, not delivered, so it won't persuade PayPal. The buyer opened this case only two days after paying, so message them that you're checking with the carrier, and plan to refund in full if delivery can't be confirmed.
